correctness.rationale: A positive unit-mass Bateman kernel is periodized exactly; its autocorrelation is explicitly integrated and periodized as a hyperbolic-sine quotient. The unique minimum of centered L2 exposure at half period follows from strict monotonicity of sinh(r y)/sinh(r L) in r for 0<y<L, proved using monotonicity of x coth(x). Rate equality follows by a smooth derivative limit, and positive unequal doses enter only by a positive product. Exact Taylor expansion gives positive quadratic phase-error coefficient. A separate standard-library checker passed 247 independent numerical assertions, without being used to infer universal validity.

originality.rationale: The exact global phase penalty, unique strict anti-phase minimizer for every positive rate pair and unequal positive dose amounts, and sharp quadratic timing-error coefficient were not located in inspected full papers, abstract-accessible close prior articles, public mathematical finding search, or available prior claim comparison. This is a best-knowledge priority assessment only: the full 1999 nonuniform-dose paper was inaccessible and a general rearrangement result may exist.
residual_risks: The full 1999 nonuniform-dosing primary article was not accessible; its abstract alone cannot rule out an equivalent quadratic phase statement in its body.
General periodic potential or rearrangement theorems could imply half-period spacing for more general kernels, even without pharmacokinetic terminology.
The theorem does not extend without proof to more than two dosing events or any nonlinear clearance or clinical objective.

value.rationale: For fixed positive doses and a period, mean steady-state exposure is phase invariant, while integrated squared variation is a natural measure of exposure smoothness. The finding solves its full positive-parameter phase optimization with a strict global ordering, a sharp closed-form phase penalty and a quantitative near-optimal tolerance, including unequal doses and equal rate constants. This gives a motivated structural classification in the classic two-stage oral pharmacokinetic model, without claiming clinical treatment or peak concentration optimality.
